# Dasuttara Sutta (DN 34 (PTS DN iii 272))

**ID:** DN 34 (PTS DN iii 272)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Dasuttara Sutta
**PTS:** DN iii 272
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0103m.mul10.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dasuttara Sutta* ("Up to Ten") is the thirty-fourth and final discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* [Norman 1983; Winternitz 1933]. Ascribed to the venerable Sāriputta, it systematically organizes Buddhist doctrine by enumerating sets of dhammas from one to ten, with ten items assigned to each number, thus totaling one hundred dharmas [Norman 1983; Winternitz 1933; Dhammadinna, ed. 2014]. The discourse represents a structured selection from the preceding *Saṅgīti Sutta* (DN 33) and anticipates the numerical and classificatory methods characteristic of the Abhidhamma [Norman 1983; Analayo 2014]. In its section on tens, it notably praises delight in the *abhidhamma* and *abhivinaya* [Analayo 2014]. Because of its analytical mātṛkā-like arrangement and shared attribution to Sāriputta, modern scholars trace close historical connections between the *Dasuttara Sutta* and early Abhidharma-oriented works, particularly the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, whose opening sections appear to draw directly upon it [Norman 1983; Analayo 2014; Potter 1996].

**Sources**

- [Norman 1983] K.R. Norman, Pali Literature (1983) — Provided details on Sāriputta's attribution, numerical structure (ten sets of ten), relationship to DN 33 and the Paṭisambhidāmagga, and Central Asian fragments.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, A History of Indian Literature, Vol. II (1933) — Explained the translation of the title and the numerical enumeration from one to ten.
- [Analayo 2014] Bhikkhu Anālayo, The Dawn of Abhidharma (2014) — Discussed the Abhidharmic character, mātṛkā extraction in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, and reference to delighting in abhidhamma and abhivinaya.
- [Potter 1996] Karl H. Potter, Encyclopedia of Indian Philosophies, Vol. 7: Abhidharma Buddhism to 150 A.D. (1996) — Noted the hypothesis connecting the nucleus of the Paṭisambhidāmagga with a commentary on the Dasuttarasutta.
- [Kuan 2008] Tse-fu Kuan, Mindfulness in Early Buddhism (2008) — Identified the Chinese translation by An Shigao (T 13) and its ten-theme framework.
- [Buswell & Lopez 2014] Robert E. Buswell Jr. & Donald S. Lopez Jr., Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism (2014) — Noted the presence of the Daśottarasūtra in the Sarvāstivāda Sanskrit Dīrghāgama and its circulation in Central Asia.
- [Dhammadinna, ed. 2014] Dhammadinna (ed.), Research on the Dīrgha-āgama (2014) — Documented the four extant recensions across schools and sectarian doctrinal discrepancies.
